text: Teodora Vasquez stood at the edge of her tomato beds with the survey map crushed in one fist, watching the man next door hammer orange stakes into soil she had turned every spring for thirty-one years. Each blow went straight up through her heels. If the fence went where those stakes said, her only gate to the back alley would be gone, and with it the path the pharmacy van used to drop off her husband's oxygen tanks. She had called the city four times. She had written two letters in her careful convent-school hand. Nobody had written back. "Please," she called across the stakes, hating how thin her voice came out. "Señor Pryce, please, just one more week. My nephew is finding the old deed, the real one." He didn't look up. She stepped forward onto the line itself, planting her slippers between two stakes as if her small body could be a boundary marker, and stayed there, trembling, while the sun climbed and the hammer went on.

I've rehearsed this conversation with Gary so many times my jaw aches from clenching it. The contractor comes Thursday. Gary wants a six-foot cedar fence, solid, no gaps, and he's within his rights, I know he is. But my son Eli climbs through the gap in the hedge every afternoon to sit with Gary's old beagle, and it's the only hour of the day Eli talks. The only hour. The therapist calls it a breakthrough. So I'm on Gary's porch with a plate of lemon bars I baked at midnight, ringing the bell twice, then a third time, wiping my palms on my jeans. When he opens the door I start talking before he can say hello. I offer to pay for the fence myself if he'll put a little gate in it. I offer to mow his lawn all summer. I hear myself offering to repaint his garage, and I can't stop, the words just keep tumbling out while he stands there holding the plate, looking at me like I've lost my mind.

The letter from the Hendersons' lawyer arrived on a Tuesday, and by Wednesday night Kwame Mensah had read it so often the folds had gone soft as cloth. A fence along the shared line, eighteen inches onto what Kwame had always believed was his side, right through the root zone of the walnut tree his late father had planted the year Kwame was born. Any arborist would tell you the tree would not survive the trenching. He had no money for a lawyer of his own. He sat at the kitchen table at two in the morning with three browser tabs open on property law, a mug of cold tea, and a legal pad covered in crossed-out arguments. His leg would not stop bouncing. Every few minutes he got up, went to the window, and looked at the dark shape of the walnut against the streetlight as though it might have moved. At dawn he was still there, dialing the number of every free legal clinic in the county, getting voicemail after voicemail.

My hands are shaking so badly I can barely hold the tape measure against the post. Maybe the surveyor was wrong. Maybe if I measure it myself, again, with the old chain my grandfather left in the shed, the line will land somewhere else. Lindqvist next door wants his fence up before the snow, and if it goes where he says, my well cap ends up on his side, and the well is the only water this farmhouse has. I measure from the oak. I measure from the corner stone. I measure from the road. Every number comes out different and none of them come out right. The ground is wet and my knees are soaked through and I keep thinking about the bank, about the appraisal next month, about what a house without its own water is worth. When Lindqvist's truck turns into his drive I scramble up so fast I drop the tape in the mud and wave both arms over my head like I'm flagging down a rescue plane.

Priya had begged the neighborhood association, the zoning office, and finally a city councilman's voicemail, and now she was down to begging Mr. Oduya himself. She caught him at the mailbox in her bathrobe, hair uncombed, because she had been watching from the window since six. "The fence will block the only light my kitchen gets," she said, and then, before he could answer, "I grow herbs there. I sell them. It's my whole income since the layoff, I can show you the books." Her voice cracked on the last word and she pressed her knuckles hard against her mouth. He shifted his weight, embarrassed, saying something about privacy, about his dogs. She nodded too fast, agreeing with everything. Could it be lower? Could it be lattice? Could she pay for clear panels at the top? She was already pulling crumpled receipts and a pencil sketch out of her robe pocket, smoothing them flat against the mailbox lid with both hands, pleading with her eyes.

I don't sleep anymore. I lie awake listening for the sound of the post-hole digger next door, though Mr. Abernathy said they won't start until Monday. Four days. Four days to find the 1962 plat map that proves the line runs where my mother always said it did. I've torn apart every box in the basement. I've called the county archive so many times the clerk recognizes my voice and sighs before I finish saying my name. This morning I drove two hours to the old title company office only to find it turned into a nail salon. I sat in the parking lot gripping the steering wheel, breathing through my teeth, because if that fence goes up eight feet to the east, the driveway I share with my disabled brother becomes too narrow for his van. He'll be stuck inside. I keep counting the days on my fingers as if one of them might turn into more. Four. Still four. I start the car and head for the next county over, to try their archive too.

The envelope said FINAL NOTICE in red block letters, and Marisol Reyes read it standing in the stairwell because her legs would not carry her the rest of the way up. Thirty days to vacate. The building had been sold. She had a son with asthma, a job that paid on the fifteenth, and eleven dollars in checking. She went up anyway, step by step, and sat on the floor of the kitchen with her back against the fridge, the paper shaking in her lap. Then she started calling. Her cousin in Fresno, no answer. The church office, closed. A housing hotline that played the same twelve notes of music for forty minutes while she chewed the skin around her thumbnail until it bled. When Mateo came in from school she shoved the letter under a dish towel and smiled so hard her cheeks hurt. Later, after he fell asleep, she spread every bill she owned across the table and counted them again, and again, as if the number might grow.

I read the letter on my phone's flashlight in the hallway because the bulb's been out for weeks and Mr. Kessler never fixed it. Rent going up forty percent on the first. I laughed out loud, a short ugly bark that echoed off the walls, and then I couldn't breathe properly. I already skip lunches. I already sold the guitar. I sat down on the top step and started doing the math with my thumb on the calculator app, and every version came out the same. So I knocked on Kessler's door. Then I pounded on it. When he opened it, I heard my voice go high and fast, promising things — I'd fix the bulb myself, paint the halls, shovel the walks all winter, anything, just hold the rent where it was for six more months. He started closing the door and I put my hand flat against it. I didn't push. I just held it there, palm pressed to the wood, saying please, please, like it was the only word I still had.

Hiroshi Tanaka had lived in apartment 4C for twenty-six years, and the letter gave him until the end of the month. Renovation, it said. Tenants welcome to reapply at market rate. He was seventy-eight. He had no car and no children and the only other place he knew in this city was the hospital. He sat at the little table by the window, where his wife used to arrange plum branches in a blue jar, and wrote a reply in pencil, erased it, wrote it again. His hand cramped. He wrote to the landlord, then to the building's management company, then to a newspaper whose address he found in an old copy by the door. He licked the stamps until his tongue tasted of glue. He walked them to the corner box in the rain without an umbrella, then stood there with his palm on the cold metal, not quite able to let go of the last envelope, whispering to it as if it could hear him.

The landlord wants proof of income by Friday or the lease won't renew, and I am lying on the bathroom floor at three in the morning because it's the only room where my roommate can't hear me. Proof. I work cash shifts at a taqueria. I have nothing printed, nothing signed, nothing with a letterhead. I've texted my manager eleven times asking if he'll write something, anything, and he hasn't answered, and every time the phone buzzes my whole body jolts and it's just a game notification. I press my forehead to the cool tile. I think about my little sister, who just started at the school three blocks away, who finally has friends, and I scroll through screenshots of every payment app transfer I've ever gotten, trying to make them look official, cropping, re-cropping, my thumbs slick with sweat. At five I give up on sleep entirely and start drafting a letter in my manager's voice, then delete it, then type it again.

Ngozi had already read the letter on the bus, at her desk, in the break room, and in the toilet stall where she locked herself during lunch. Pets not permitted; the dog must be removed within fourteen days or the lease would be terminated. The dog was a twelve-year-old greyhound named Pilot who had slept against her back every night since the divorce. She spent her lunch hour calling every pet-friendly building in the city and got a waiting list, a waiting list, a laugh, and a three-thousand-dollar deposit. Her coffee went cold beside the keyboard. By evening she was knocking on the property manager's office door with a printed letter from her doctor, a photo of Pilot asleep on a cushion, and a check for an extra month's rent she could not actually afford. Her fingers left damp prints on the photo. "He doesn't bark," she kept saying while the manager read. "He's too old to bark. Please. He doesn't even bark."

Dmitri read the notice twice, then turned it over as if there might be some other answer printed on the back. The building was being converted to condos; every tenant had sixty days. His mother lived with him now, after the stroke, and the ground-floor unit with the wide bathroom door was the only place in the neighborhood her wheelchair fit. He paced the length of the living room, eight steps, turn, eight steps, the paper rolled into a tube he kept tapping against his thigh. From her chair his mother asked what it said, and he told her it was about the recycling. Then he went into the bedroom, shut the door, and called the tenants' union, the city housing office, an attorney he'd seen on a bus ad. He left voicemails in a low, rushed voice, giving his number twice in each, spelling his last name letter by letter. When he came out, he made her tea with hands he could not keep still.

The departure board flipped from DELAYED to CANCELLED and Amara felt her knees go loose. Her father was in the ICU in Lagos. The doctor had said hours, maybe a day. She ran, actually ran, rolling bag clattering behind her, to the service desk, where forty people were already in line. She cut to the front and nobody stopped her because of whatever was on her face. "I need any flight," she said. "Any route. Through Paris, through Istanbul, I don't care, I'll sit in the toilet, please." The agent typed. Amara watched the woman's eyes on the screen and tried to read them. She had her phone pressed against her other ear, her brother on the line, his voice crackling: still breathing, still breathing. Her free hand gripped the edge of the counter so hard the laminate bit into her palm. When the agent said tomorrow morning, Amara made a sound she didn't recognize and asked her to look again.

Gate 14. Four hours delayed, then six, and the interview is at nine tomorrow morning in Denver, the first one in eight months that went past a phone screen. I've already called the recruiter twice. I've already looked at every rental car, every bus, every other airline flying out tonight, and I keep refreshing the same three apps in a loop, my thumb moving on its own. The battery is at nine percent. I crawl under a row of seats to reach the one working outlet and sit there on the gross carpet, knees to chest, cord stretched tight, while a toddler stares at me. If I miss this I don't know what happens with the lease. I don't let myself finish that thought. Instead I start rehearsing my answers under my breath, quietly, in case I have to do the interview on a phone in a bathroom stall, and I write a list of every possible flight number on the back of my boarding pass in tiny cramped letters.

Old Mr. Castellano had been standing at the gate desk for twenty minutes, long after the agent had stopped answering him. His granddaughter's wedding was at four o'clock in Boston. He had a suit bag over one arm and a small box tied with ribbon in the other hand, and the board said the flight would not leave until five-fifteen. He kept explaining, in his slow, careful English, that he had promised to walk her down the aisle because her father was gone, that she had no one else to do it. He held up the box as if it were evidence. The agent's face was kind and tired. Behind him, the line shifted and muttered. He asked about standby, about another airline, about whether a pilot might be persuaded. His voice kept rising and catching. Finally he sat down on the nearest chair, set the box on his knees, and dialed his granddaughter's number with a thick, unsteady finger, rehearsing an apology he could not bear to say.

They've moved us three times now, gate to gate, and I've carried a sleeping four-year-old through every terminal of this airport. My arms are on fire. Sami's medication is in the checked bag, the bag is somewhere on the tarmac, and his next dose was due an hour ago. I've told the gate agent, the supervisor, a man in a reflective vest, and a woman at the information booth who just pointed me back to the gate agent. My voice has gone hoarse. I keep pressing two fingers to Sami's neck while he sleeps, feeling for something, I don't even know what. Every time he shifts I hold my breath. Finally I lay him across two seats and stand on a chair, actually stand on it, waving my boarding pass at a passing pilot, calling out to him, while people look up from their phones. I don't care. I'd climb onto the luggage belt and ride it out to the plane if somebody would just tell me which one it was.

Five hours into the delay, Rafael Ortiz had stopped pretending to read. He was supposed to sign the papers on his late brother's house at noon, the only day the buyer would close, the only way to clear the debts that had followed him home from the funeral. He had calculated it out on a napkin at the food court: miss tomorrow and he lost the sale, lose the sale and the bank took the house. He paced the length of the terminal and back, past the same chocolate shop, the same sleeping backpacker, the same broken escalator. He tried bribing a man to swap seats on a different flight and got a disgusted look. He called the buyer's agent and left a message, then a second one, his voice tight and too loud. Around midnight he found himself at an empty gate, forehead pressed to the cold glass, staring at a plane he wasn't booked on, mouthing numbers to himself.

I've been awake for thirty hours and the flight to Seoul has been pushed again, and my sister's surgery starts in fourteen. She asked me to be there when she woke up. I promised her. I keep pulling up her last text, just the word ok and a heart, reading it until the letters blur. My eyes sting from the fluorescent lights and my mouth tastes like metal. I've gone to every airline desk in this terminal asking about seats. One agent offered a route through Vancouver that would get me in two hours after she wakes; I told her to book it, then changed my mind, then begged her to book it again when the next delay posted. Now I'm standing by the gate with my shoes off because my feet are too swollen, watching the board without blinking, as if staring hard enough might hold the numbers in place. Whenever a pilot walks past I search his face for some sign that we're about to go.

The doctor said the word positive and then a lot of other words that Jae-won couldn't hear over the rushing in his ears. He nodded at all of them. He kept nodding. When the doctor stopped talking he asked her to say it again, slower, and wrote it down this time on the back of a parking receipt, the pen skidding across the paper. Treatment options. Clinical trial. Insurance approval. He asked about the trial three times. He asked if there was a waiting list and how long, and whether calling every morning would help, and whether she knew anyone, anyone at all, who could move him up. His leg jittered under the desk hard enough to shake her pen cup. In the parking garage he sat in his car without starting it and called his insurance company, then his brother, then a cousin in Seoul who was a nurse, talking fast, reading the parking receipt aloud, asking each of them what to do next.

The results are in the portal. I can see the little red flag beside them from the login screen, and I can't make my finger click it. I'm in my car outside the pharmacy, engine running, heater blasting, and I'm still cold. When I finally open it, it's a column of numbers I don't understand, and three of them are bold. I google every one. Every result is worse than the last. I call the clinic and get a recording. I call again and press zero over and over until a human picks up, and I hear myself talking too fast, begging her to have the doctor call me today, not Monday, today, I can't do the weekend like this. She says she'll leave a note. I ask her to read the note back to me. My hand is cramping around the phone. After she hangs up I keep holding it to my ear, listening to nothing, staring at the bold numbers until they swim.

Grandmother Oyelaran had walked forty minutes to the clinic in her good shoes, and now she sat very still while the young doctor explained that her kidneys were failing and dialysis would be three times a week, at a center across the city. She had no car. Her daughter worked nights. The bus took two transfers. She asked whether there was a pill instead, and the doctor gently said no. She asked about a center closer by. No. She asked whether, if she ate differently, if she drank only water and gave up salt and prayed harder, it might be slower. The doctor didn't answer that one. Her fingers worked at the clasp of her handbag, open, shut, open, shut. On the way out she stopped at the reception desk and asked the girl there if she knew anyone who drove, a neighbor, a church member, anybody, and she would pay, she would cook for them, she would do whatever they asked.

I keep reading the letter in the hallway of my apartment because I can't make myself go into the kitchen where my wife is cooking. The biopsy came back. Stage three. There's a specialist in Houston who does a new procedure, and the referral coordinator said the waitlist is four months, and four months is the number the letter says I might not have. I sit on the stairs. I call the specialist's office and get a voicemail, call back and press every extension until somebody answers. I tell them I'll take any cancellation, any hour, I'll fly out on a moment's notice, I'll sleep in the lobby. My voice keeps climbing and I can hear it echo in the stairwell. When the scheduler says she'll put me on the list, I make her repeat my name, my number, my date of birth. I make her spell it. Then I go upstairs, wash my face, and smile at my wife like nothing's wrong.

Lucía clutched the printout against her chest the whole walk from the lab to the parking lot. Her daughter's bloodwork was wrong. Not a little wrong. The pediatric oncologist could see them in nine days. Nine days. She had read online about what could happen in nine days, and she had not stopped reading since. In the car she called every children's hospital within a three-hundred-mile radius, scrolling through the list on her cracked screen with a trembling thumb, asking each one for the soonest opening. She spelled her daughter's name eight times. She offered to drive overnight. She offered to wait in the ER. Her breath came short and shallow, and she kept twisting around to look at Sofía buckled in the back seat, happily coloring, her small tongue poking out in concentration. Lucía pressed her palm flat against her own sternum to slow her heart and dialed the next number on the list.

Arjun was on hold with the genetic testing company for the third time that morning, listening to the same loop of piano music, his laptop open to a spreadsheet he'd built at four a.m. listing every specialist in the state who handled the mutation. The result had come back by email. A gene name and a percentage. Seventy-two percent lifetime risk. His twins were six. He couldn't stop picturing their faces when they asked about Grandpa, who had died of the same thing at fifty. He had already canceled two meetings. He hadn't eaten. Every few minutes he refreshed his inbox in case the genetic counselor had answered, then refreshed it again. When a human finally picked up, he cut her off before she finished her greeting. He wanted to know if the test could be wrong. He wanted a retest. He wanted to pay for it today. He'd drive the sample there himself if that would make it faster.

The red sixty-one at the top of the page made Tomasz feel like the floor had tilted. He needed a seventy-five to keep the scholarship. Without it, no tuition, no dorm, no visa. He read the margin comments with his face so close to the paper his breath fogged it. Then, before the classroom emptied, he was at Professor Hale's desk, the exam held out in both hands like an offering. He started explaining his reasoning on question four, how he had nearly had it, how the method was almost right. He asked whether partial credit could be reconsidered. He asked about extra credit, a makeup essay, a second exam, anything. His accent thickened the faster he talked, and he could hear it, and that made him talk faster. Hale said he'd take a look. Tomasz thanked him four times, backed out of the room, then stood in the hallway clutching the paper, unable to make himself walk away.

I flipped the paper over and there it was, a forty-three, circled twice like the teacher wanted to make sure I saw it. Dad said if I failed chemistry again I'd have to quit the team, and the regional final is in two weeks, and the scouts are coming. I shoved the exam into my backpack so fast I tore the corner. All through the rest of class I couldn't hear a word. My ears were ringing. When the bell went I waited by Ms. Okafor's door until everyone else was gone, and then I asked if I could retake it, and when she said no, I asked about a project, a report, anything, I'd stay after school every day, I'd come in Saturdays. My voice went weird and wobbly and I hated it. She said she'd think about it. I said thank you, thank you, way too many times, and then I walked to the bathroom and stood in a stall staring at the forty-three until I'd memorized every wrong answer.

Mrs. Delacroix handed back the bar exam practice sets in alphabetical order, so Benedict had a long time to watch everyone else's faces before his turn. When he finally got his, it was the lowest score yet. The real exam was in nineteen days. His firm had made it clear: pass this sitting or the offer was withdrawn. He had already failed twice. He sat in his car in the parking lot afterward, pulling up flashcards on his phone, scrolling through them so fast he couldn't possibly be absorbing anything. He opened his calendar and started deleting things: his mother's birthday dinner, a friend's wedding, the dentist. He made a plan to study eighteen hours a day. He wrote it out on a legal pad, hour by hour, until the pen ripped through the page. Then he started over on a fresh sheet, even smaller handwriting, squeezing in more hours, scribbling notes until it grew too dark in the car to see.

The grade was a D-plus, and under it, in neat green ink, the teacher had written: see me about the scholarship requirements. I knew what that meant. I sat there with the paper face-down on my desk and my palms flat on top of it, as if holding it down could stop the grade from being real. My mother cleans offices at night so I can be the first one in the family to go to college. That's the sentence I kept hearing in my head, over and over. After class I went to the teacher's office and stood outside for ten minutes before knocking. When she opened the door I couldn't get a full sentence out; I just held up the paper and asked what I could do, what was left, was there any way at all, and my chin started shaking and I had to stare at the ceiling. She pulled out a chair for me. I sat on its very edge, ready to do anything she said.

Yusuf watched Professor Lindgren walk down the rows handing back the final exams, and by the time she reached him his shirt was stuck to his back. Twenty-eight out of a hundred. His whole medical school application rode on this class. He didn't move. When the room cleared he was still sitting there, then suddenly on his feet, catching her at the door, talking over himself. He'd had the flu that week, he could get a note. His grandfather had been in the hospital. He'd studied, he swore he had, he could show her his notes, three notebooks full. He pulled them from his bag, one after another, flipping pages at her, diagrams, color-coded tables, until she gently put a hand on the stack to stop him. He asked for an incomplete. He asked for a retest. He asked if he could audit the course again for free over the summer. She said she'd consider it, and he nodded, and kept nodding, swallowing hard.

The exam was folded in half when Ms. Petrakis set it on my desk, and I knew. I knew before I opened it. Thirty-five. Mum had said that if I didn't bring up maths this term she'd pull me out of the after-school art program, which is the only place I ever feel normal. I put my head down on my arms and breathed the smell of the old wooden desk and tried to think. Then I sat up and started going through it question by question with a pencil, redoing every problem in the margins, my handwriting getting messier and messier. If I could show her I understood it now, maybe she'd change the mark. I worked straight through lunch. When the bell rang I carried the scribbled-over exam to her desk, every margin crammed with workings, and asked her, voice cracking, whether this counted for anything, whether it could count for anything at all. My stomach was knotted so tight I couldn't stand up straight.

Colm saw Declan by the bananas and his first instinct was to push his half-empty cart around the corner and hide. Then he remembered that Declan ran a construction firm now. Colm had been out of work for seven months. The mortgage was three payments behind. So he abandoned the cart and caught up with him near the bread, too fast, nearly clipping his heel. "Dec! God, it's been, what, fifteen years?" He laughed too loud. They talked about school, about the old hurling team, and the whole time Colm's mind was racing, looking for an opening. When Declan mentioned a big job starting in the spring, Colm grabbed his arm. He didn't mean to. He let go and apologized and then said he could do anything, drywall, hauling, sweeping, he'd start tomorrow, he'd work weekends, he'd take less than the others. He heard his own voice cracking in the cereal aisle and couldn't stop it.

I almost didn't recognize Haruka in the frozen foods aisle, and then I did, and my heart started pounding so hard I had to grip the cart handle. She's a transplant coordinator at St. Agnes. I'd read that online, a year ago, and never had the nerve to call. My husband has been on the kidney list for three years. So I said her name, and when she turned and smiled I was already talking, telling her everything, the dialysis, the matches that fell through, the way he sleeps sitting up now. I knew she couldn't do anything. I knew it the whole time I was talking. But I kept going, standing in the cold air from the open freezer door, clutching a bag of peas against my chest until my fingers went numb, asking whether there was anything, any list, any trial, any name she could give me, while she held her basket and looked at me with that careful, kind expression that made me want to cry.

The checkout line was long, and Beatriz recognized the woman two carts ahead as Celeste, her college roommate, the one she'd stopped answering when things got bad. Celeste had money now; you could see it in the coat, the bag, the organic everything. Beatriz looked down at her own cart, a loaf of bread, rice, the cheapest eggs, and the envelope in her purse from the utility company with the shutoff date circled. She stood there biting the inside of her cheek, rehearsing. Could she ask? After eight years of silence, could she just ask? Celeste reached the register. Beatriz abandoned her cart in line and went forward, her face burning, touching Celeste's sleeve. They hugged. Celeste said all the right things. And then Beatriz heard herself saying it, low and fast, eyes on the conveyor belt: four hundred dollars, just until the end of the month, she'd pay it back with interest, she'd sign something, she was so sorry to ask, so sorry.

Sunil hadn't left the house in three weeks except for groceries, and he had built the trip into a ritual: one store, the quiet one, at eleven at night, in and out. So when Marcus Bell turned into the canned-goods aisle, Sunil froze with a can of lentils in each hand. Marcus had been his best friend at twenty. Marcus didn't know about any of it, about the divorce, the drinking, the job, or the empty bottles under the sink. Marcus was smiling and saying his name and opening his arms, and Sunil walked into the hug and couldn't let go. He gripped the back of Marcus's jacket. He felt his shoulders start to shake. Marcus said hey, hey, easy, and Sunil said he was sorry, he was fine, he was just tired. Then he asked, still holding on, whether Marcus had any time, tonight, now, even for a coffee, because he really didn't want to go back to the house alone.

When I saw Yara by the deli counter my whole body went hot, because Yara is the only person besides my parents who knows where my brother might be. They dated, right before he disappeared. Eleven months since anyone's heard from him. I left my basket on the floor and practically ran to her. She saw my face and took a step back. I don't blame her. I said, "Have you heard from him? Anything? A text, a call, a friend of a friend?" She said no, she was sorry, she'd told the police everything already. I didn't believe her, or I didn't want to, and I kept asking the same questions in different ways, did he ever mention a city, a name, a job. I pulled out my phone and showed her his photo, as if she'd forgotten his face. People were staring. The deli man had stopped slicing. I couldn't make myself stop asking.

Wilhelmina was reaching for the cheapest coffee on the bottom shelf when someone said her maiden name, and she straightened up to find Abigail Thorne, from the old church choir, beaming at her. Abigail's son was a judge now. Wilhelmina knew that from the papers, and she knew, too, that her grandson's sentencing was Friday. She had prayed over it every night. Now God had put Abigail in the coffee aisle, and Wilhelmina couldn't waste it. She took both of Abigail's hands in her own, squeezing them hard, the coffee can tucked under her arm. She asked after the family, after the choir, and then her voice dropped and her words came out tangled: her grandson was a good boy, he'd made one mistake, he had a baby daughter, could Abigail's son just look at the file, just one look. She could see the alarm rising in Abigail's eyes, and she held on to her hands anyway, unable to let go.

The engine coughed twice and died on the overpass, and Nadia steered onto the narrow shoulder with cars screaming past close enough to rock the frame. Seven forty-two. The shift started at eight, and her supervisor had said, very clearly, one more late arrival and she was done. She turned the key again. Nothing but a clicking. Again. Clicking. She slammed her palm on the steering wheel, then pressed both hands over her mouth. She called her sister; voicemail. She called a cab company; twenty-five minutes. She called the supervisor and hung up before it rang. Then she got out, popped the hood, and stared at the engine as if she could understand it if she just looked hard enough. Her work shoes slipped on the gravel. She started flagging down passing trucks with both arms, stepping farther into the lane than was safe, her blouse plastered to her back in the wind, shouting at windshields that didn't slow down.

Steam was pouring out from under the hood and I was on a two-lane road in the middle of nowhere, forty minutes from the plant, with no signal. Today is the day the regional director is visiting. Today was supposed to be the day I proved I deserved to keep my position after the layoffs. I stood on the roof of the car holding my phone up to the sky, turning slowly in circles, watching for one bar. Nothing. I climbed down and started walking toward the farmhouse I could see maybe a mile off, then started jogging, then running in dress shoes on a dirt shoulder. My chest burned. My tie whipped back over my shoulder. When I got to the porch I knocked so hard the screen door rattled in its frame. An old man opened it, and before he could say a word I was asking for his phone, his truck, a ride, anything, I'd pay him whatever he wanted.

Abuela's old Buick gave out at a red light on Fifth Avenue, and Esteban, nineteen and on his way to the first day of his first real job, sat there with horns blaring behind him. He tried everything he'd seen his uncle do. Pumped the gas. Jiggled the shifter. Prayed out loud in Spanish. Nothing. People were shouting from their windows. He got out and tried to push it to the curb by himself, one hand on the frame, one on the wheel, his new white shirt soaking through. A bus swerved around him. He kept checking his phone between shoves: 8:52, 8:53, 8:54. The orientation began at nine sharp, and they'd made it clear no one would be admitted late. He finally got the car to the curb, abandoned it with the hazards blinking, and started running, his tie flapping, his lungs burning, the borrowed shoes slipping on his heels with every stride.

I'm on my knees in a gas station parking lot at six in the morning trying to change a tire with a jack that doesn't fit this car. My hands are black. I've scraped two knuckles open. The nursing home where I work has six residents on my wing who need their morning medications at seven, and the overnight nurse leaves at seven whether I'm there or not, and the agency has nobody else. I keep thinking about Mrs. Albescu's insulin. The lug nuts won't budge. I stand on the wrench, bounce on it, feel it slip and nearly fall. I'm talking to myself now, out loud, come on, come on, please. A man getting gas watches me for a while and then walks over, and I look up at him and I can't even manage a hello, I just hold out the wrench to him with both hands and ask if he can help, please, I've got to get to work, people need me.

Kofi's car shuddered and quit in the left lane of the expressway, and he coasted, hazards on, toward an exit he wasn't going to make. Somewhere behind him a semi blasted its horn. He was due in court at nine as the only witness for his cousin's defense, and the public defender had told him plainly that without him the case was finished. He got the car onto the median, a strip of dry grass and litter. He called the attorney's office with sweat stinging his eyes, got an assistant, explained, begged her to tell the judge, to ask for an hour, half an hour. Then he opened the ride-share app and watched the little car icon creep toward him, refreshing the arrival estimate every few seconds, shifting from foot to foot, checking the time, checking the icon, checking the time again, a cold knot sitting high under his ribs.

The battery light flickered once and then the whole dashboard went dark, and Ilse coasted to a stop beside a cornfield with the dawn barely starting. She had a presentation at nine that her whole team had spent four months building, and she was the one carrying the slides. She dug through the glove compartment for jumper cables she knew she'd lent out last month. She tried calling her husband, who was on a night shift with his phone in a locker. She tried calling a coworker, who didn't pick up. Her breath came in short puffs of white in the cold. She got out and stood in the middle of the empty county road, phone in hand, watching both directions for headlights, so cold her teeth chattered. When a pickup finally appeared over the rise she stepped right out in front of it, waving the laptop bag over her head, not caring if it stopped hard.

It was 2:14 when Gwendolyn checked the clock again, and Theo's curfew had been midnight. She had called his phone so many times it went straight to voicemail now, his cheerful recorded voice saying leave a message, over and over. She had texted every friend whose number she had. She'd called the Petersens, waking them, apologizing, asking if Theo was there. He wasn't. She stood at the front window with the curtain clutched in one fist, watching headlights sweep past and not turn in. Every time one slowed, her heart leapt. She paced the hallway in her socks, picked up her car keys, put them down, picked them up again. Where would she even drive? She opened his bedroom door and looked at the unmade bed and the sneakers kicked into the corner, then shut it fast. She called the local hospital and asked, in a voice that didn't sound like hers, if any teenage boys had been brought in tonight.

My daughter's location dot stopped moving at 11:40 at an address I don't recognize, out past the quarry, and it's 1:30 now and it still hasn't moved. Her phone rings and rings. I'm in my coat, sitting on the bottom stair, keys in my hand, because I've decided three times to go and three times decided to wait in case she walks in. I zoom in on the dot until the map goes blurry. It's a field. Just a field. My hands won't stop trembling and I've bitten my lip hard enough to taste blood. I call her best friend's mother, who sounds annoyed and then frightened. I call my ex-husband, who doesn't answer. I stand up. I sit down. Finally I go, driving with the map propped on the steering wheel, the window down so I can hear, calling her name out into the dark before I'm even close enough for her to possibly hear it.

Rustam had never been a man who waited well, and tonight he could not sit at all. His son Daler was seventeen, had borrowed the car at eight, and had promised to be home by eleven. It was nearly three. Rustam had walked the length of the apartment so many times that his wife, from the bedroom, had stopped asking him to come lie down. He'd driven the route to the boy's friend's house twice and found nothing but dark windows. Now he stood on the balcony in the cold, in his undershirt, gripping the rail and leaning out over the street so far that a passing neighbor called up to ask if he was all right. He waved them off. Every engine sound pulled him forward. He was bargaining under his breath now, in Uzbek, words his own grandmother used to say, promising things to God he had no right to promise, if only the boy came home.

I've cleaned the whole kitchen. Twice. It's the only thing my hands can do. Jada said she'd be home by ten, and it's past one, and she's not answering, and the last thing I said to her was that if she wore that jacket she looked like trouble. That's the last thing. I keep scrubbing the same spot on the counter. I keep checking my phone face-down on the table, flipping it over, flipping it back. Her location's turned off. I went through her room an hour ago looking for anything, a name, a note, and found nothing but a birthday card from me she'd saved, and now I can't stop thinking about it. I call her again. I hear myself leaving the message, saying I'm not mad, I'm not mad, please just call, I'll come get you anywhere, no questions, baby, anywhere. Then I sit down on the kitchen floor with the sponge still in my hand and wait.

The rain had started around midnight, and by two Siobhan had put on her boots and her husband's raincoat and gone out to the end of the drive, because standing in the house was unbearable. Callum was sixteen and had only had his license a month. He'd gone to a party on the other side of the lake, on the twisting road with no guardrails. She stood under the dripping streetlight with her phone cupped in both hands to keep it dry, calling him every couple of minutes, listening to it ring through. Water ran down her neck. She walked up the road a little way, then back, then up again, as if she could meet him halfway. When headlights appeared around the bend, she stepped out into the road with her arms raised, then saw it was a delivery van and stepped back, her legs nearly folding. She dialed the number again, lips moving, her face wet with more than the rain.

Every time a car passes I'm out of my chair before I know I've moved. It's 3 a.m. My son Mateusz should have been home at midnight. He's never late, not once, not even five minutes, which is what's making this so much worse. I've called the police and they told me teenagers stay out all the time and to call back in the morning. I told the officer my son is not that kind of teenager and he said they all say that. I've walked every street in a six-block radius in my slippers. I've called his coach, his friend Ola, his friend Ola's parents, who are now also awake and also calling people. My chest feels like it's being squeezed by a fist. I sit by the front door with my back against it so I'll feel it if he tries to come in, the porch light on, the phone in my lap, rocking a little, unable to keep still.

The email just said: Please come see me at 3. No subject line. Femi had read it at 10:15 and had done nothing useful since. Rumors about layoffs had been circulating for weeks, and he was the newest on the team, and his wife was seven months pregnant and on his health insurance. He spent his lunch hour updating his résumé in a private browser window, glancing over his shoulder. At 2:40 he went to the bathroom and splashed water on his face, then stood gripping the edges of the sink, looking at himself, practicing: I can take on more accounts. I can take a pay cut. I can work weekends. At 2:58 he was outside the manager's door. When she said come in, he went in already talking, offering to transfer departments, to go part-time, to do anything at all that would keep the insurance active until the baby came, his folder of performance reviews clutched against his chest like a shield.

The manager closed the door behind me, and that's when I knew. They don't close the door for good news. I sat down and pressed my knees together to stop them from shaking. He started talking about restructuring, about difficult decisions, and I cut in before he could say it. I told him I'd made mistakes on the Hollis account but I'd fixed them. I told him about the overtime I'd put in, the weekends, the client in Phoenix who'd asked for me by name. I could hear my voice getting faster and higher. I said I had two kids, that my husband's hours had been cut, that we'd just signed a lease. I said I could take a demotion, any role, the front desk, the mail room. He kept trying to slide a folder across the desk toward me and I kept not taking it, because as long as my hands weren't on it, maybe it wasn't happening yet.

Ah-young had been with the company eleven years, and when the HR assistant came to her desk and said Mr. Brennan would like a word, she stood up so fast her chair rolled into the filing cabinet. She knew about the audit. She knew the missing funds had passed through her approval queue, though she had not taken them; she'd signed off on a vendor invoice that looked legitimate. She'd been sleeping two hours a night going through old records trying to find proof. Now she walked down the corridor with her printouts in her arms, the stack so thick she had to hold it with her chin. Inside Brennan's office she spread them across his desk before sitting, pushing them toward him, pointing at highlighted lines, the vendor number, the date, the second signature, her finger shaking on the page. "Please," she said. "Please just look at this one. And this one. Look at this one first."

I've been sitting outside Monique's office for twenty-five minutes because she's on a call, and the waiting is worse than whatever she's going to say. My visa's tied to this job. If I'm let go I have sixty days to find another sponsor or leave the country, and my daughter's in second grade here, and she doesn't remember any other home. I keep reading the nameplate on the door. I keep straightening my cuffs. I've opened my phone to the immigration lawyer's number a dozen times and closed it. The receptionist offered me water and I said yes and then didn't drink it; it's sitting on the little table getting warm. When the door finally opens I stand up too fast and knock the cup over, and I'm on my knees mopping it up with my sleeve, apologizing over and over, while Monique says it's fine, it's fine, come in.

Old Pieter Van Dam had driven the delivery truck for the bakery for twenty-two years, and he knew the new owner's son had been wanting him gone. When he was called into the little office behind the ovens, he took off his cap and held it in both hands, turning it round and round by the brim. The young man began to talk about efficiency, about a delivery service app. Pieter interrupted him. He knew every customer by name, he said, the café on Groenstraat that wanted their rye sliced, the old woman on the hill who couldn't get to the door fast. He'd come in earlier. He'd take Sundays. He didn't need a raise. His pension was still four years off and his wife's medicines were not cheap. The cap kept turning. His voice, which had been steady for years of predawn routes, began to wobble, and he stared hard at the floor so the boy wouldn't see his eyes.

Leilani's manager pinged her at 4:52 on a Friday: got a minute? Come by my office. She stared at the message so long her screen dimmed. She had been on a performance improvement plan for six weeks. Today was the last day of it. She had worked every night, rewritten her reports, sent her manager hourly updates she suspected nobody read. She stood up and sat back down. She opened her sent folder and started scrolling, searching for every thank-you email, every bit of praise, anything she could bring in as evidence. She printed nine of them. The printer jammed. She yanked the paper out, tore it, and reprinted, her face hot, her coworkers glancing over. When she finally walked to the office she had the pages fanned in her hand like cards, rehearsing under her breath what she would say first, and second, and third, and what she'd say if he didn't let her speak.

The envelope was tucked inside a hatbox at the very back of the attic, and the handwriting on it stopped Rosalind's breath: her mother's, addressed to a man named Anton at an address in Kraków, never sent. Inside, her mother had written that the baby was his. Rosalind was the baby. She read it on her knees in the dust, then read it again, the paper crackling in her grip. Her mother was gone. Her father, the man she'd called father, was gone. Was Anton? She scrambled down the ladder so fast she missed a rung and slammed her shin. At the kitchen table she typed the name and the old address into every search engine, every genealogy site, every Polish phone directory she could find, the letter flattened under a bowl so her trembling hands wouldn't tear it. It was past two a.m. when she started drafting emails to strangers with the same surname, asking each one if they knew him.

I found it in a shoebox under the eaves: a letter from my grandfather to a bank in Zurich, dated 1971, listing an account number. My aunt had always said he'd hidden money before he died. We'd laughed about it. Now the house is being foreclosed on in five weeks and there's a slip of yellowed paper in my hand with a number on it. My knees are pressed into the rough attic boards and I can't stop reading the number out loud. I take a photo of it, then three more, then go downstairs and make a photocopy, and then another, and put them in different places around the house in case one disappears. I call the bank's international line and sit through an automated menu in German, pressing buttons at random. I call my aunt and talk so fast she has to ask me to start over. I keep touching the original letter to make sure it's still real.

Behind a stack of old tax returns, Chidi found a letter from his father, written the year before the accident, addressed to Chidi himself and never given to him. It said: I know about the debts. I am trying to fix it before you find out. If something happens to me, there is a man named Okonjo in Enugu who owes me, find him. The letter was nineteen years old. Chidi sat on the attic floor with his back against a rafter, the paper on his knees, his heart thudding hard enough that he could feel it in his throat. The family had lost the house, his mother had worked herself sick, and all along there had been a name. He went through every other box in the attic that night, ripping tape, dumping contents, looking for anything else, a phone number, another letter, an address, his hands filthy with dust, sneezing, refusing to stop until he'd opened every single one.

The letter fell out of a book of poems when I was clearing my late husband's things, and it wasn't from me. Darling, it began, in a woman's handwriting, and it was dated the summer before we married. It said there was a child. I sat down hard on an old trunk and the dust rose up around me in the slanted light. Fifty-two years of marriage, and somewhere there might be a son or daughter of his, in their fifties now, who never knew him, whom he never mentioned. I need to know. I need to know before my own heart gives out, before the doctors' estimate runs down. I turned the envelope over and over looking for a return address, a postmark, anything. There was a smudged stamp from Galway. I took a magnifying glass from the desk downstairs and spent an hour over that smudge, holding it to the window, tilting it, squinting, begging the ink to give up one more letter.

Jun-seo was up in the attic looking for the Christmas lights when he found the letter his late wife had written to him and never given him, folded inside a box of her sewing patterns. My love, it began, there's something I need you to know before the doctors tell you. The rest of the page had been water-damaged; the ink had bled into gray clouds and only a few words were legible. Sorry. Hospital. Ask Mi-ra. He held it under the bare bulb, then took it downstairs to the kitchen and held it under the brightest lamp he owned, then put on his reading glasses, then took them off. He tried the trick with a pencil rubbing he'd seen on television. He called Mi-ra, his wife's sister, who hadn't spoken to him since the funeral. It rang and rang. He called again, and again, sitting on the stairs, clutching the ruined page to his chest.

In the corner of the attic, under a moth-eaten quilt, I found a letter my mother wrote to her sister in 1989, and in the second paragraph she mentions, almost casually, that she'd given the baby up in Leeds, and she hoped it had gone to good people. I'm an only child. I've always been an only child. I'm on the floor with the quilt still in one hand and the letter in the other and I can't get enough air into my chest. My mother has dementia. On good days she knows my name. My aunt died last spring. There is no one left to ask but her, and every week there's less of her left to answer. I'm already getting up, already climbing down the ladder, letter in my teeth, already grabbing my keys to drive to the care home tonight, before she slips any further, before whatever she still remembers about Leeds is gone for good.

The roast came out of the oven gray in the middle and black at the edges, and the doorbell was going to ring in eighteen minutes. Fernando stared at it. His fiancée's parents were driving in from Monterrey to meet him for the first time, and her father had made it clear on the phone that he did not think a line cook was good enough for his daughter. Tonight was supposed to prove otherwise. Fernando grabbed his knife and started carving away the charred crust, trying to salvage the center, slicing thinner and thinner. He threw a pan on the burner for a sauce that might hide everything. The smoke alarm went off. He climbed onto a chair and fanned it with a dish towel, coughing, then jumped down and burned his wrist on the pan handle without stopping. Butter, garlic, wine, too much wine. He kept tasting with his finger, shaking his head, adding more, glancing at the clock.

The guests are the board of the restaurant group that's deciding whether to fund my place, and they'll be here at seven. It's 6:41 and the soufflés have collapsed. All twelve of them, sunk into their ramekins like little craters. I don't have the eggs to start over. I'm standing in my kitchen in my chef's whites with my hands braced on the counter, breathing through my nose, while my sous chef Rina watches me with her mouth half open. "Okay," I say. "Okay, okay." I'm opening every cabinet. I'm pulling out flour, cream, an old jar of praline. I'm going to make something else, I don't know what yet, something with what we have. My hands are moving faster than my brain. I'm telling Rina to run to the corner store for eggs, to beg the bakery down the street for anything they have left, to just go, go, go, I'll figure it out.

Mrs. Adebayo had cooked for her husband's colleagues before, but never for the department chair, and never on the night his tenure decision was being made. The jollof had stuck to the bottom of the pot and the whole kitchen smelled of scorched rice. She had forty minutes. She scraped the top layer into a clean pot, tasting, wincing, adding stock, tomato, pepper, praying the burnt taste would fade. It didn't. She called her sister in Houston on speaker, stirring with one hand and holding the lid with the other, and her sister told her what their mother used to do, a slice of onion on top, cover it, wait. She did it. She lifted the lid every thirty seconds to sniff. Her husband came in to ask if he should open the wine, and she shooed him out with the spoon, her eyes stinging, telling him everything was fine, it was perfect, go and set the table, please.

I dropped the cake. The whole thing, three layers, upside down on the kitchen tile, frosting smeared in an arc toward the dishwasher. My in-laws arrive in twenty minutes for my mother-in-law's sixtieth birthday, which I insisted on hosting, after she'd said, in front of everyone at Easter, that I couldn't even boil an egg. I'm on my knees with a spatula, scooping. Some of the middle layer is fine. I could restack it. I could cover the damage with fruit. I'm putting pieces on the plate and they're crumbling and I keep pressing them together with my fingers, smoothing frosting over the cracks with the back of a spoon, my heart going so hard I can hear it in my ears. There's frosting in my hair. My husband texts that they're early, they're parking now. I shove the whole plate into the fridge, slam the door, lean against it with my eyes squeezed shut, and try to think.

The gas went out ten minutes before the guests were due, the burners guttering to nothing with the pasta water barely warm, and Aurelio stood there turning the knobs back and forth as though that would bring the flame back. It was his first dinner as the new owner of the trattoria, an invitation-only opening for the critics and investors who would decide if the place lived or died. He had sunk his father's savings into it. He called the gas company and got a recorded message about outages in the district. He ran out the back door and banged on the neighboring café's kitchen door, explaining in a rush, offering to pay for their stove time, any amount, just for an hour. The owner shook his head. Aurelio came back and began hauling out a camping stove from storage, kneeling on the floor to fit the canister, his fingers fumbling, his apron dragging in the dust, as the first knock sounded at the front.

The guests were due at eight and at 7:35 Hamid opened the fridge to discover the fish he'd been marinating all afternoon smelled wrong, sour, sharp, unmistakable. His girlfriend's brother was a chef in Paris. Hamid had spent two weeks planning this dinner to win him over, to show he was serious about her. He threw the fish in the trash and then stood over the bin, hands on his head. What else did he have? Eggs. Rice. A sad bag of spinach. Half a lemon. He tore through the pantry knocking cans to the floor, reading labels, discarding them. He called three restaurants for takeout and none of them could deliver before nine. He grabbed his wallet and his coat and ran down the stairs to the market on the corner, praying it was still open, pushing through the door just as the clerk was flipping the sign, holding up both hands, pleading for five minutes, only five.

The moving truck pulled away and only then did Oksana realize the box with her papers was not among the ones stacked in the empty apartment. Passport, work permit, the offer letter, her grandmother's ring. All of it. She turned in a circle among the cardboard, tearing open lids, flinging out towels and dishes and shoes. Not there. She ran down four flights of stairs and out into the unfamiliar street, the city loud and indifferent around her, and saw the truck turning the far corner. She ran after it, in sandals, shouting, waving, people stepping aside to stare. It was gone. She stood on the curb heaving for breath and dialed the moving company, and the dispatcher put her on hold, and she paced the sidewalk in front of a building she didn't know, in a city where she knew no one, repeating the truck's license plate under her breath so she wouldn't forget it.

The key the landlord mailed me doesn't fit. I've tried it upside down, I've jiggled it, I've pushed and pulled and leaned my whole weight against the door. It's nearly midnight, I've just driven nine hundred miles, and my cat is yowling in her carrier at my feet. The landlord's phone goes straight to voicemail. I've left four messages, each one shakier. I start on the other tenants, knocking door to door down the hallway, apologizing, asking if anyone has a number for the super, a spare key, anything. Most don't answer. One man swears at me through the door. I sit down on the floor of the hallway with my back against my own locked door, holding my cat carrier in my lap, and pull up hotel listings on my phone, and every one within reach costs more than what's left in my account until payday. I try the key again. And again. My fingers are raw from it.

Moving to Toronto had been Gabriel's idea, all of it: the job, the apartment, convincing his wife to leave her mother behind in Belo Horizonte. Now, two days in, the job had fallen through. The company had frozen hiring, a terse email said, and his offer was rescinded. He hadn't told Luiza yet. She was in the other room unpacking the good dishes, humming. He sat on the edge of the bare mattress with his laptop on his knees, applying to everything, warehouse jobs, delivery, call centers, typing his credentials over and over into form after form with fingers that kept hitting the wrong keys. Each time Luiza called out to ask where something should go, he answered too cheerfully, his voice pitched strangely high. The lease was signed for a year. Their savings would cover two months, maybe. He kept refreshing his inbox, refreshing, refreshing, his jaw so tight his teeth ached.

I've been in this city four days and I've just learned that the apartment I signed for, paid for, and moved into isn't legal. The real owner showed up this morning with a police officer. The man I wired the deposit to doesn't exist; his number is disconnected. I have until tonight to get out. My boxes are still taped shut in the corners, and I'm standing among them with my phone pressed to my ear, calling the bank's fraud line, on hold for the forty-first minute, while I scroll rental listings on my laptop with my other hand. I don't know a single person here. I keep turning toward the window as if someone I know might walk past. My stomach's been churning since dawn. When the hold music cuts out I start talking before the agent can finish her greeting, explaining everything in one breath, asking if there's any way, any way at all, to get the money back today.

Wen hadn't eaten since the flight, and now she stood in the lobby of a building in Lyon that did not match the photographs, being told by the concierge in rapid French that the unit she'd rented had been given to someone else. Her French was textbook French. She kept asking him to repeat himself, slower, s'il vous plaît, pulling out the printed contract, pointing at the signature, the dates, the stamp. He kept shrugging. Her suitcases leaned against her legs. It was raining outside, and the doctoral program started Monday, and her stipend wouldn't arrive for three weeks. She took out her phone and opened a translation app, typing with shaking thumbs, holding the screen up to his face so he could read it: Please. I have nowhere else. Please call the owner. Please. When he waved it away, she typed it again, larger, and held it closer.

Three weeks into his new life in Chicago, Tobias Engel opened his mailbox to find a letter from his landlord giving him ten days to produce a co-signer or vacate. He'd moved for a job that paid well on paper, but his credit was thin and he knew nobody in the state. He went upstairs and sat on a folding chair in his nearly empty apartment, and made a list on the back of the envelope of everyone he could possibly ask. It was a short list. An old roommate who'd moved to Dallas. A college professor. An ex-girlfriend's father, who'd liked him once. He called each of them, one after another, rehearsing his opening line out loud first. He hated how small his voice got when they picked up. When the last one said no, he stared at the bare walls for a long time, then picked up the phone again and started calling his coworkers, whom he barely knew.

Mile twenty-five, and Chiara's left hamstring had been seizing for the last two. She'd been training four years to break three hours, to qualify for Boston, and her watch said she had nine minutes left to cover the final mile and change. She could do that. She'd done it a thousand times. But her leg was a rope pulled tight and every stride felt like stepping on a knife. She was making a noise with each breath now, a sort of whimper she couldn't control. She grabbed a cup at the water station and threw it on her face. She pinched the back of her thigh hard, pressing her thumb in to make the cramp let go, still moving, half hobbling, half running. Runners she had passed an hour ago went by her. She kept her eyes on the green digits of her watch, counting under her breath, telling her leg please, please, just six more minutes, please.

I don't have anything left. I'm four-tenths of a mile from the finish and my body has simply stopped listening. My dad's out there at the line, in his wheelchair, wearing the shirt I printed with my mom's face on it, because this was her race, she ran it nine times, and I promised her in the hospice I'd finish it. I promised. My legs are wobbling under me like a newborn calf's. I've stopped sweating, which I know is bad. People on the sidelines are yelling my name off my bib and I can't lift my head. I go down on one knee. I get up. I go down again, and this time I crawl a few feet before I can stand. A volunteer reaches for my arm and I shake her off, because if she helps me, it doesn't count, and I have to make it count. I keep moving toward the noise.

Gideon had placed eleventh in this marathon three years running, and the sponsorship contract that paid his rent required a top-ten finish. He was in twelfth now, last mile, with tenth just fifteen meters ahead. The gap wasn't closing. His lungs were full of broken glass and the taste in his mouth was copper. He dug into reserves he wasn't sure he had, pumping his arms harder, his stride going ragged and wide. The man in eleventh glanced back and saw him coming and surged, and Gideon gave a hoarse shout of frustration and surged with him. The crowd was a blur of color and noise. He didn't feel his feet anymore. He fixed his eyes on the yellow singlet in front of him and pictured the eviction notice taped to his door last winter, the empty fridge, his mother's worried voice on the phone, and pushed until his vision started narrowing to a tunnel.

My calf has gone into a cramp so hard I can see it bunched under the skin like a fist, and I'm standing at the side of the course clutching a lamppost with the finish arch visible, maybe twelve hundred meters away. I raised nineteen thousand dollars for the children's ward by promising I'd finish this race. Twenty-two of those kids made me a banner. They're at the finish. They're holding it right now, waiting for me. I can't let them watch me get carried off. I pound on the muscle with my fist. I stretch it against the curb, nearly crying from the pain. A medic jogs over and asks if I want to stop and I say no, no, no, I'm good, I'm fine. I take a step and almost fall. I take another. I start walking, then shuffling, gritting my teeth so hard my jaw clicks, thinking of the banner, the crayon letters, their names.

The pace runner Nikolai was supposed to follow had pulled away at mile twenty-three, and now, with a mile to go, he was alone and slowing and his watch was blinking a time that would miss the Olympic qualifying standard by seconds. Seconds. He had sold his car to afford the altitude training camp. He had moved back in with his parents at thirty-one. He drove his elbows back harder, lifted his knees, ignored the stitch under his ribs that felt like someone had slid a blade between them. The roar of the crowd seemed distant, underwater. He started bargaining with himself in short, choked phrases: to the next corner, to the next sign, to the man in the red shorts. His shoelace had come undone and he didn't stop for it. His eyes kept going to the watch and back to the road, the watch and the road, the seconds slipping away faster than his feet could follow.

The sweep bus was rolling up behind Mercedes, and everyone knew what that meant: anyone it passed was pulled off the course. She was sixty-four, it was her first marathon, and she had told everyone at the cancer center she was going to finish. Everyone. She had walked the last six miles. Her toenails were bleeding into her shoes. She could hear the bus's engine idling closer, a low patient rumble. She broke into a jog that was barely faster than a walk, her arms pumping crookedly, her breath sobbing out of her. She looked back once, saw the headlights, and forced herself faster. Her hip screamed. A teenager on the sidewalk started running beside her, cheering, and she couldn't even turn her head to thank him. The finish clock was still a blur in the distance. She kept muttering her grandchildren's names, one per step, as if they were pulling her forward on a rope.

Biscuit had been out in the yard for ten minutes when Harriet realized she couldn't hear his tags jingling anymore. She called his name from the back door. Nothing. She stepped out barefoot onto the frost-hard grass and called again, louder. The gate on the far side was swinging open in the wind, its latch broken, the way she'd been meaning to fix all autumn. Biscuit was fourteen and mostly deaf and half blind. The road beyond the gate was a county highway where trucks went past at sixty. She ran through the gate in her nightgown, calling, her feet burning on the gravel, and stood at the edge of the road looking both ways into the dark. A truck roared by and the wind of it nearly knocked her over. She screamed his name into its wake. Then she ran back for a flashlight, came out again, and started down the ditch, sweeping the beam through the weeds, calling and calling.

It's been forty minutes. I let Juno out after dinner like always, and she always scratches at the door after five, and tonight she didn't. I've walked the yard with a flashlight three times. I've checked under the deck on my belly, the light jittering across spider webs. I found a gap under the back fence where the dirt's been dug out fresh, and that's when my stomach dropped, because past that fence is the woods, and past the woods is the interstate. I've texted every neighbor. I've posted on the community page with her photo, my fingers stabbing at the keyboard. Now I'm pushing through the woods in my slippers, branches tearing at my face, shaking her treat bag, calling her name in that sing-song voice she loves, except my voice keeps breaking halfway through and it comes out wrong. Every rustle in the leaves I spin toward. Every rustle is nothing. I keep shaking the bag.

Ezekiel's son had cried himself to sleep, and now Ezekiel was out in the dark yard alone, flashlight in one hand and the dog's leash in the other, because he had promised the boy he would find Rufus before morning. The dog had slipped out through a hole in the hedge sometime after supper. Ezekiel had already driven every street in the subdivision twice with the windows down, calling. Now he was crawling along the hedge on his knees, shining the light into every gap, the damp soaking through his trousers. He found a scrap of fur on a branch and held it under the beam for a long time, turning it, as if it could tell him which way. Then he widened the circle. The neighbor's shed, the drainage culvert, the ditch by the bus stop. He kept checking his phone, hoping someone had answered the post, and kept whistling the two-note whistle Rufus always came to, until his lips went numb.

Maeve had been out in the rain for an hour with a can of cat food rattling against a spoon, because that was the only sound Lady ever came running to. The dog was a rescue, terrified of everything, and if she'd bolted she would be hiding somewhere, frozen, refusing to come out even for her own name. Maeve had already searched every bush in the yard, every corner of the garage, the space beneath the porch where she'd scraped her shoulder raw squeezing in. Now she was out on the street, soaked to the skin, knocking on doors. Have you seen a little brown dog? She's scared, she won't come to you, just call me, please, any hour. She pressed slips of paper with her number into strangers' hands, so many that she ran out and started writing it on the backs of her receipts. Her teeth were chattering. She kept rattling the spoon against the can, a lonely sound in the empty street.

I keep going back to the spot where his leash snapped. Just a frayed clip, lying in the grass by the fence post. The neighbors' kids were setting off fireworks and Captain is so scared of fireworks, and when I came out to check on him he was gone. That was two hours ago. I've walked the entire neighborhood. I've called animal control, the emergency vet, the shelter's after-hours line, which only plays a recording. Now I'm in the car, driving at five miles an hour with my hazards on and the windows down, calling his name into the dark, scanning every yard, every shadow under every parked car. My throat is raw. I keep imagining the highway. I keep pushing the picture away. A man on the sidewalk shouts that he saw a big dog heading toward the creek and I swerve the car to the curb so hard the tires scrape, and I'm out and running before I've even turned off the engine.

Nobuko's husband had left the yard gate open when he went out for cigarettes, and Hana, their little white terrier, had not come in when Nobuko called her for supper. Nobuko was eighty-one. She walked with a cane. She went out anyway, into the twilight, along the narrow lane between the houses, calling Hana's name in a thin, wavering voice. Her husband came back and joined her, apologizing, and she couldn't even look at him. She went down to the river path where Hana loved to chase ducks, leaning hard on the cane, her breath coming in short gasps. When the cane slipped on a stone and she went down on one knee in the mud, she didn't get up right away. She stayed there, peering into the reeds along the bank, calling, calling, her hand outstretched toward the water as though the little dog might come out and lick it, the way she always had.

The stage manager said two minutes, and Lucien could not feel his fingers. He had played this concerto a hundred times in rehearsal. But tonight the conductor of the Berlin orchestra was in the third row, and Lucien was thirty-four, old for a soloist, and if this didn't go well there would be no more chances; his agent had told him so in almost those exact words. He stood in the wings flexing and unflexing his hands, then shoved them under his armpits to warm them, then held them under the hot-water tap in the green-room sink until they turned red. Not enough. His left pinky felt like wood. He rubbed it between his palms, blew on it, pressed it against his own neck. The applause for the opening piece swelled and faded. He was mouthing the first eight bars to himself, eyes squeezed shut, his whole body leaning toward the stage as though he could drag his hands back to life by force of will.

The bassist didn't show. The bassist, our bassist, the one person in this band who can actually keep time, and the showcase starts in twelve minutes, and there's a label scout in the back booth who we've been chasing for two years. I've called Dex nine times. I've texted him in all caps. The other two are staring at me like I'm supposed to fix this, and I'm the singer, I'm just the singer. I'm running around the green room asking every other band if anyone plays bass, if anyone knows our songs, if anyone has even heard of us. A kid in a beanie says he can sort of play. I grab him by both shoulders. I don't care if he sort of plays. I'm already scribbling the chord changes on a napkin for him, my pen tearing through it, talking faster than he can listen, promising him a cut of whatever we make, promising him anything.

Zainab's violin string snapped in the warm-up room ten minutes before her conservatory audition, the one she'd flown across an ocean for, the one her family had sold her late father's car to pay for. The E string, the one she'd forgotten to pack a spare of. She stared at the curled wire hanging from the peg. Then she was out the door and running the halls, knocking on rehearsal rooms, asking anyone holding an instrument case if they had a spare E. Most shook their heads. One laughed. She tried the front office and they had nothing. Her heart was hammering in her throat. Down by the elevators a cellist said he thought there was a music shop two blocks away. She checked her watch. Eight minutes. She ran. In the street, in her black recital dress and flat shoes, she ran, her hair coming loose from its pins, nearly colliding with a man walking a bicycle.

I'm standing in the wings and I've forgotten the second verse. Completely. It's not there. It's my own song, the one I wrote about my father, and I've sung it in my car every day for a month, and now there's a white hole where the words should be. In four minutes I walk out in front of two thousand people, and my label has told me pretty plainly that tonight decides whether they keep me on. I grab a stagehand and ask her for a pen, and I write the first line I can remember on my wrist, and then I start whispering the song to myself from the top, fast, praying the verse will come back with the momentum. My mouth is dry as paper. I gulp from a water bottle and spill it down my shirt. Nothing. The chorus, the bridge, and that empty gap. I press my forehead against the cool brick and keep whispering.

Old Ignatius had not played in public for twelve years, not since the tremor started, and tonight he had agreed to play at his granddaughter's wedding because she'd asked him, crying, and he could not refuse her. Now he sat in the vestry of the church with his accordion on his lap, and his right hand was shaking so badly the buttons clattered. He pressed it hard against his knee. He held it with his left. He breathed the way the physical therapist had shown him, in for four, out for eight, and the hand still shook. He took the pills from his breast pocket and swallowed two, which was one more than the doctor allowed. He could hear the guests filling the pews. He began playing scales, quietly, over and over, the same few notes, forcing his fingers onto the right buttons, his lips moving in what might have been a prayer, sweat running down into the collar of his good suit.

Five minutes before the recital, Esperanza realized her sheet music was still in the taxi. The piece was by a contemporary composer, forty pages of irregular rhythms that she had never once played from memory. She dumped her bag out on the green-room floor, pawing through lip balm and tissues and keys. She called the taxi company and was put on hold. She ran out to the lobby where the patrons were filing in and asked the box office staff if they had a printer, if they could find the score online, anywhere, any edition. Her accompanist hovered behind her, pale. Esperanza sat down at the green-room upright with her eyes shut and tried to play the opening from memory, stumbling, starting over, stumbling, starting over. Her hands were slick. Through the wall she could hear the house lights' warning chime, and she kept trying, kept restarting, as if the notes would come if she just pounded hard enough.

The package had no return address, just Ingrid's name in block capitals and a postmark from the town where her estranged son had last been seen. She hadn't heard from Anders in six years. She tore the tape with her fingernails, ripping the cardboard in long ragged strips, and found inside a cheap phone, a charger, and a folded note: Keep this on. I'll call when I can. Don't tell anyone. Her hands went cold. She plugged the phone in right there on the hallway floor, not even bothering to take off her coat, and sat cross-legged beside the outlet, watching the battery icon fill. She checked that the ringer was on. She checked again. She turned the volume all the way up and then tested it by calling it from her own phone, twice, just to hear it ring. Then she didn't move. She didn't eat. She sat on the floor in her coat into the night with the little phone in both palms.

It was addressed to my late wife, and inside was the medication she'd ordered from some overseas pharmacy the month before she died, along with an invoice for four thousand dollars, past due, in red. I didn't know. I didn't know she'd been buying it, or that she'd been that frightened, or that she'd been hiding it from me.
