I sat at the kitchen table with the pill bottles lined up in front of me and the invoice flattened under my palm, and I read the fine print until my eyes burned. Collections in ten days. I already owe the hospital more than the house is worth. I called the number on the invoice and it rang somewhere in a time zone where it was the middle of the night. I called again. I wrote an email, deleted it, wrote another, begging, explaining she was gone, asking if they'd take the unopened bottles back, asking anything at all.

The box on Kenji's doorstep was from an address in the city where his younger sister had been living before she stopped answering his calls three weeks ago. Inside were her favorite sweater, the watch their father had left her, and a stack of photographs of the two of them as kids. Nothing else. No note. He tipped the box upside down and shook it. He felt along the seams. He went through the sweater pockets, turning them inside out. He held each photograph up to the light and turned it over, looking for a word, a date, anything written on the back. There was nothing. His breathing had gone shallow. He grabbed his phone and called her number, which went to a disconnected-line recording, and then the police in her city, and the man who answered asked him to slow down, slow down, because Kenji was talking so fast the words were tripping over each other.

I didn't order anything. That's the first thing I keep telling myself. The box is small and heavy and it's from the law firm handling my divorce, and inside is a thumb drive and a printed letter that says my ex-husband's lawyers are going to use what's on it at the custody hearing on Thursday. I put the drive in my laptop with my heart in my mouth. It's photos of me from two years ago, the worst year, the year I don't talk about. My hands go numb. Thursday. Three days to find a lawyer who can answer this, and the one I have doesn't return calls for days. I'm calling every family attorney within fifty miles, scrolling down the list on my phone, getting machines, leaving my number in a voice I barely recognize. Upstairs, my daughter is singing in the bath. I put my fist against my mouth so she won't hear anything through the floor.

Thandiwe opened the unexpected parcel standing at the mailbox and found a jar of her grandmother's peanut sauce, the label in her grandmother's own handwriting, and a note from a hospice in Durban saying the old woman had asked for it to be sent before she was moved to the end-of-life wing. It had taken three weeks to arrive. Thandiwe's whole body went rigid. She left the mailbox hanging open and ran inside, dropping her keys twice on the way to the door, and started calling the hospice, but the line was busy, and then busy again. She pulled up flights on her laptop while the phone redialed beside her. Johannesburg, then Durban. Twenty-six hours, maybe more. She booked the first one without checking the price, then sat on the edge of the sofa with the jar clutched in her lap, rocking, listening to the busy signal, whispering to the jar to hold on, hold on, I'm coming.

The package Feodor found on his step was a refund. His prototype, the hand-built espresso machine he'd spent his savings on, sent back by the trade show with a note saying his exhibition application had been rejected for missing paperwork. The show was in nine days. Every investor he'd been chasing would be there. He stood in the doorway in his slippers with the box half open, reading and rereading the letter, his mouth moving silently. Missing paperwork. Which paperwork? He dragged the box inside and ripped into his filing cabinet, scattering folders across the floor, spreading permits and receipts and correspondence in a wide fan around him until there was no carpet left showing. He found the form. It was there. It was right there, signed, dated. He called the organizers' office with the form crumpled in his fist, and when the receptionist said the deadline had passed, he started reading the form aloud to her, line by line.

The ring wasn't in the jewelry box. Bronwyn went through it twice, lifting every brooch and tangle of beads, while her brother Rhys stood at the window watching her. Their grandmother had promised that ring to Bronwyn when she was nine, a sapphire set in old gold, and Bronwyn had planned for months to sell it. She had to. The clinic had told her that the fertility treatments would stop without the next payment, and this round was the last chance her body had. She went through the dresser next, drawer after drawer, pulling out stockings and handkerchiefs and letting them fall. Rhys asked if she was all right. She said she was fine, she was just looking. She checked the pockets of every coat in the wardrobe. She upended a sewing basket and pins scattered across the floorboards. She was on her hands and knees, running her palms along the dusty floor beneath the bed, when Rhys knelt down and said her name quietly.

My sister and I agreed we'd split everything fairly. But Gran's house has to be sold, and the buyer's offer expires Friday, and my sister wants to keep it. I've already spent my half. I didn't tell anyone. I borrowed against it six months ago when the business started going under, and if the sale doesn't close, the people I borrowed from aren't the kind who send letters. So I'm in Gran's sewing room pretending to sort buttons while my sister goes through photo albums and cries, and I'm trying to find the right moment, the right words. My palms are slick. I've rehearsed this all morning in the car. When she holds up a picture of us on Gran's porch and says she can't bear to let this place go, I hear myself say she has to, she has to, and my voice comes out much too loud, and she looks at me, startled, and I can't take it back.

The three of them had agreed not to fight. But when Mariela found the shoebox of letters in the bottom of their grandmother's closet, and saw the name of the family lawyer on top, she clutched it to her chest before her brothers could see. She'd read one page. Just one. The will they'd all been given was not the most recent one. There was another, and if it was what she feared, everything was going to Aldo, who'd stopped visiting Abuela years ago, and Mariela, who had cared for her every day through the long last year, would have to leave the house she'd been living in, with her two children, and nowhere to go. She went into the bathroom and locked the door and sat on the edge of the tub, reading the letters with shaking hands, searching for a date, a signature, some sign it was a draft, some reason it might not count, the steam pipe ticking behind her.

Grandma's diary is the only thing I wanted. Not the jewelry, not the furniture, not the house. Just the green leather diary from 1956, because it's the only place anyone ever wrote down who my real grandfather was, and my doctors need family medical history for the transplant evaluation, and without a name I'm stuck at the bottom of the list. My cousins are going through the closets and I'm turning out drawers in the study, flipping through every notebook, every ledger, every recipe card she ever kept. It's not here. It's not in the bookshelf. It's not in the trunk. I ask my cousin Ilana if she's seen it and she says Aunt Rhoda took a box of books to the donation bin yesterday. I'm already putting on my coat, asking which donation bin, where, what time, and she's looking at me like I've lost my mind, and maybe I have, but I'm already running for my car.

Grisha had come back for one reason, and he didn't tell his sisters what it was. Their grandmother had kept cash in strange places, everyone knew that, rolled into stockings, sewn into cushions, slipped between pages of books. He owed money to a man who had stopped being patient, and he had until Sunday. While Katya and Olga folded tablecloths and wept over old photographs, Grisha moved from room to room squeezing pillows, shaking out books, running his fingers along hems. His sisters noticed. He saw them noticing. Still he kept going, his jaw clenched, his face flushed, unable to stop himself. When he found the seam in the old armchair that had been resewn with different thread, he took out his pocketknife and slit it right there in front of them, and Olga gasped, and he didn't look up. He just dug his hand deep into the stuffing, feeling around, breathing hard, praying.

The quilt was the thing. Not valuable, just faded squares of calico, but it was the only thing Nell's youngest daughter asked for when Nell told her Great-Grandma had passed: Mummy, can I have the sleepy blanket? Nell's daughter was in the hospital, eight years old, and the nights there were long and loud and frightening, and Nell had promised. Now her brother said he'd already given the quilts to the charity shop with the rest of the linens. Nell stood in the bedroom staring at the stripped bed. Then she was in the car, her brother still calling after her, driving across town to the charity shop with her hazard lights on, parking crookedly on the curb, going through the bins of donated linens in the back room with the volunteers watching her nervously. She was pulling out every blanket, every coverlet, unfolding each one and shaking it open, saying no, no, not that one, faster and faster.

Abdul unlocked the shutter on Monday and the smell hit him first: water. The pipe above the stockroom had burst over the weekend, and two inches of it covered the floor, soaking the bottom shelves of rice sacks and flour and the boxes of spices he'd ordered from Karachi with the last of his line of credit. He stood in the doorway in his good shoes, the water seeping in over the leather, then waded in and started hauling sacks onto the counter, one after another, his arms straining. Some split open in his hands, wet rice spilling. He called the landlord: voicemail. He called the insurance agent: the office opened at ten. He called his son, who said he'd come after class. Abdul didn't stop moving. He carried what he could to the dry front room, stacking boxes on chairs, on the counter, on the windowsill, trying to save whatever could still be saved, his breathing loud in the echoing shop.

I turned the sign to OPEN at nine sharp like I have every Monday for six years, and nobody came. Nobody. Not the old man for his newspaper, not the school moms for coffee. Then I saw it across the street: the new chain store, grand opening, balloons, a line out the door. My bank loan payment is due in two weeks and I've been short every month since spring. I stood behind the counter rearranging the pastries, then rearranging them again. I wrote 50% OFF on a piece of cardboard with a marker that was running dry and taped it to the window, crooked. I went out onto the sidewalk with a tray of free samples and stood there in the cold, holding it out to people walking past, smiling until my face ached, saying good morning, good morning, try one, please, they're fresh, I baked them myself at four this morning.

The lock had been broken. Valentina saw it before she was halfway down the block: the door ajar, the glass smashed, the jagged edges glinting in the Monday sun. Inside, the register drawer hung open, empty. The display case of silver jewelry, her own work, three years of it, was gone, every piece. She stood in the middle of the floor crunching glass under her boots and couldn't make her lungs work. Her insurance had lapsed in March because she'd skipped a payment to cover rent. She knew that. She'd known it every day since. She called the police and gave the report in a flat, thin voice. Then she started walking the neighborhood, checking every pawn shop that opened at ten, showing her phone photos of the pieces, her hands trembling so much the clerks had to steady the screen. At the fourth one she saw her own cuff bracelet in the case and pressed both palms flat against the glass.

It's Monday, and the health inspector is coming at noon, and I just opened the walk-in fridge and the compressor's dead. Everything in there's warm. Milk, meat, the cream for the pastries, all of it. If the inspector writes us up again after last month's violation, the city shuts us down, and this deli is everything my father built, and it's mine now, and it's already barely surviving. I start dragging crates out to the alley, throwing out everything that could possibly fail a test. Then I'm on the phone to the refrigeration repair company, begging for anyone, any technician, today, this morning, I'll pay double, triple. I'm on the phone to the supplier, asking for an emergency delivery. I'm on my knees in the walk-in with a flashlight, poking at a compressor I don't understand, reading a manual on my phone. Sweat is running into my eyes. My father's photo watches me from the wall above the slicer.

Every Monday for twenty-three years, Mr. Prakash Iyer had opened the bookshop at eight and put the kettle on. This Monday he opened it at seven, because the landlord's letter said the lease would not be renewed unless he could pay the new rent by the end of the month, and the new rent was triple. He'd been up all night with his accounts. Now he was dragging tables out onto the sidewalk and stacking them with books, everything at a dollar, the rare first editions too, because he needed money and he needed it now. He made signs by hand and taped them to lampposts up and down the street. When the first customer came by, a student with headphones, Mr. Iyer followed him along the tables, pointing out titles, offering two for one, then three for one, his voice too eager, his smile too wide, the student edging away from him with an uncertain little wave.

Rosa Montoya pulled up the metal grate of her little flower shop on Monday morning and found a notice taped to the inside of the glass: the city was shutting down the street for eight weeks of construction starting tomorrow. No parking, no foot traffic, the sidewalk torn up. Eight weeks. Mother's Day fell in the middle of it. That was a third of her year's income. She tore the notice down and read it standing in the doorway with the buckets of roses waiting behind her, still wrapped from the market. She called the city office and was transferred four times. She called her councilwoman. She called the newspaper. She called her suppliers and canceled the big order, then called back and uncanceled it, then canceled it again. By ten she had started an online shop on her phone, building it with her thumbs while standing at the counter, photographing bouquets against the wall, her hands shaking so much the pictures came out blurred.

The line outside the food bank stretched around the block by eight, and Odalys, on her third Saturday volunteering, was watching the shelves empty faster than she could restock them. The truck from the regional warehouse hadn't come. There would be nothing left for the people at the back of the line, and she could see them from the window: a man with three kids, an old woman on a walker, a teenage girl holding a baby. Odalys ran to the coordinator, who was on the phone with the warehouse, shaking her head. Odalys went into the storeroom and started tearing open boxes that had been set aside for next week, then the emergency reserve, then the donations nobody had sorted yet. She was pulling cans out by the armful, checking dates, dropping some, apologizing to no one. When those were gone she grabbed her own car keys and her own debit card and asked a volunteer to come with her to the supermarket.

I came to volunteer at the food bank. That's what I told my wife. That's what I told myself. But I've been laid off four months now and the fridge at home is empty and my kids have been eating cereal for dinner, and while I'm stacking cans in the back I keep looking at the bags we're handing out. I'm not supposed to take anything, I know that. Volunteers sign a form. I keep picking up a jar of peanut butter, putting it down, picking it up. My face is burning. When the coordinator asks if I'm okay I say yes too fast. I go out to the parking lot and sit in my car and grip the steering wheel and try to breathe. Then I go back inside, stand in front of the coordinator's desk, and ask, in a voice that I can barely get out, whether there's any way I could also sign up to receive.

Mrs. Kowalczyk had organized the Thanksgiving turkey drive at the food bank for eleven years, and this year, two days before the holiday, she discovered that the freezer had failed overnight. Two hundred turkeys, thawed and warm, spoiled. Two hundred families who had been promised one. She stood in front of the open freezer door in her apron, the smell rising around her, and then she was moving. She called every grocery store manager in the county. She called the bishop. She called the radio station and asked them to put out an appeal on air, her voice cracking as she spelled out the address. She went to the bank and withdrew money from her own savings, the account she'd been keeping for her funeral, and the teller asked twice if she was sure. She was sure. By evening she had driven to three counties in her old station wagon, filling it with whatever birds she could buy, refusing to rest.

The girl came in with a younger brother on her hip and asked, very quietly, if we had baby formula. We didn't. We hadn't had it for weeks. I'm only seventeen, I'm here for my service hours, and I've never felt like this, like something was clawing up my throat. She couldn't have been older than me. The baby was making a thin, weak sound, not even crying properly. I told her to wait, please wait, don't leave, and I ran through the back storeroom checking every shelf, every box, every bag, even the ones marked expired. Nothing. I ran to the coordinator, who was out, and then to the other volunteers, asking if anyone had formula at home, anyone at all. Nobody did. I took out my phone and started calling my mother, my aunt, the pharmacy around the corner, my voice tumbling over itself, and the whole time I kept checking that the girl was still sitting by the door.

Thursday's distribution had been going smoothly until the generator died and the lights went out and the walk-in cooler went silent. Babatunde, who'd been volunteering there since he retired from the post office, knew exactly how long they had before everything inside started to spoil: maybe four hours. There was more fresh produce in there than they'd had in months, donated by a farm co-op, a once-in-a-season gift. He got on his phone and started calling every volunteer on the contact sheet, asking them to come, now, with coolers, with ice, with cars. He hauled crates of lettuce and peppers out to the shade of the loading dock himself, his back screaming. He flagged down people walking past on the sidewalk and pressed bags of vegetables into their hands, asking them to take them, take more, take them home, please, before they wilt, before we lose them. His shirt was soaked through and he didn't slow down.

I volunteer every Wednesday, and every Wednesday Mr. Fitzgerald comes in for his bag, and today he didn't. Ninety-one, lives alone, no phone. He hasn't missed a Wednesday in two years. By the end of the shift I can't stop looking at the door. The coordinator says he probably just slept in, but I don't believe that, and when we close I drive to his building with his bag on the passenger seat. I knock on his door. Nothing. I knock harder, then pound, then call his name through the letterbox, my mouth right against the cold metal. I can hear the television. I run down to the building manager's office, and it's closed. I'm going door to door, asking neighbors if anyone has a key, a number, anything, my voice getting louder and higher with each door. One woman says she thinks his nephew lives in Ohio. I keep knocking. I keep calling through the letterbox.

They had taken Elif's husband through the swinging doors four hours ago, and nobody had come out to tell her anything since. She sat on the hard plastic chair at first. Then she stood. Then she went to the desk and asked the nurse, politely. Then she went back twenty minutes later and asked again, less politely. She had called his brother in Ankara twice and couldn't make herself call a third time because she had nothing new to say. The waiting room television played a cooking show nobody watched. Elif twisted her wedding ring around and around her finger until the skin beneath it was raw. Every time the doors swung open she leapt to her feet, searching faces, and every time it was someone else's doctor calling someone else's name. Finally she stood right beside the swinging doors, close enough to look through the little window, her hand pressed flat on the painted wood as if she could feel through it to him.

The surgeon told us six hours, and it's been nine, and nobody will tell me why. I've drunk five cups of the vending-machine coffee and my hands won't stop shaking, though I don't know if that's the caffeine. My boy is in there. He's twelve. He fell off the roof of the garage, the roof I told him a hundred times to stay off of, and I wasn't watching because I was on the phone. I keep going over that. Over and over. I've been to the desk six times. The nurse has started looking at me with that particular patience they save for people they're worried about. I've texted everyone I know asking them to pray, even the ones who don't pray. I'm pacing the length of the waiting room, counting the floor tiles. Forty-two. I turn and count them again. Forty-two. If I count them enough, maybe the door will open.

Dr. Ramachandran had been a physician for thirty years, which made it worse, not better. He knew too well what the delay meant. His wife's surgery should have been over at noon. It was nearly four. He sat in the family waiting area like any other husband, his white coat left at home, and found he could not sit still. He stood and walked to the window. He came back. He called a colleague who worked on that floor and asked, in a carefully neutral voice, whether he'd heard anything, and the colleague said he'd go look. Then nothing. Twenty minutes. Thirty. Ramachandran's knee bounced. He kept pressing his thumbnail into the pad of his index finger, harder and harder, until it left a white crescent. When he heard footsteps in the corridor he rose halfway out of his chair. A janitor with a cart. He sat back down, put his face in his hands, and started reciting a prayer he hadn't said since boyhood.

My brother's blood type is rare, and the hospital doesn't have enough. They told me this an hour ago, in a quiet room with a box of tissues on the table, and they told me they were calling around, other hospitals, the regional bank. So I've been calling too. I've posted on every social network I have, begging, typing his blood type in capital letters, my fingers jabbing at the screen. I've called his friends, my friends, our church, my old university's alumni office. I sit in the waiting room and my phone is hot in my hand. Every time someone replies I read it so fast I misread it. Strangers are sharing the post. One says she's a match and she's on her way, and I start crying right there in the plastic chair, loudly, in front of everyone, and then I make myself stop, because she isn't here yet, and he's still in there, and it's not enough, it might not be enough.

Old Augustin Mbeki had been in the waiting room since dawn, his cap twisted into a knot between his hands. His granddaughter had gone into labor too early, much too early, and they had rushed her into surgery, and then a team had rushed out with an incubator, and then nobody had told him anything. He did not have a phone. He did not know how to reach the baby's father, who worked on a ship somewhere at sea. Every time a nurse passed, he rose stiffly from his chair and stepped into her path, hat in hand, and asked in his halting English whether there was news. They were kind. They didn't know. He started following one of them down the corridor until she gently turned him back. He went to the chapel, knelt on the cold tile on his old knees, prayed, then hurried back to the waiting room in case he had missed someone calling out his name.

I've been sitting in this waiting room for three days, going home only to shower. My mother's in a coma. The doctors say every day that passes makes waking less likely, and tomorrow they want to talk to us about what they keep calling options, which I know is the word they use before they say the other word. I haven't slept more than two hours at a time. I've read every article I can find on my phone about people who woke up after weeks, after months, saving them in a folder to show the doctors. I've written down questions in a notebook, pages of them, numbered. When the night nurse walks by I ask her about a specialist I read about in Boston, and whether he could be consulted, and whether the hospital would call him, and whether I could call him myself. She says she'll ask. I write that down too, underline it twice, and keep reading.
